title: Neuve, douce, fraîche et longue
summary: Form useful feminine adjectives by family while learning exceptions individually.
objectives: Form feminine `-f`, `-c` and `-oux` adjectives with their exceptions.
Use `frais`, `long`, `favori` and `rigolo` in all gender/number forms.

sources.label: Public A2 index: topic-coverage reference only

sections.title: The ending can change, not just gain `e`
paragraphs: An adjective describes a noun and normally agrees with its gender and number. Many masculine adjectives ending in `-f` replace `f` with `ve` in the feminine: `neuf/neuve` (new), `actif/active` (active), `sportif/sportive` (sporty), `vif/vive` (lively), `veuf/veuve` (widowed). To form the plural, usually add `s` to each gender form.

Adjectives ending in `-c` do not have one universal feminine rule. Learn `blanc/blanche` (white), `franc/franche` (frank), `sec/sèche` (dry), `public/publique` (public), `turc/turque` (Turkish), `grec/grecque` (Greek), `caduc/caduque` (no longer valid). Notice `sec` changes both spelling and accent, while `grec` keeps `c` before `que`.
points: Complete models: `neuf, neuve, neufs, neuves`; `public, publique, publics, publiques`; `grec, grecque, grecs, grecques`.
Some less common `-f` words such as `bref/brève` have an accent change too; do not use the simple family rule as a substitute for a dictionary when unsure.

examples.french: La serviette est **sèche** et la nappe est **blanche**.
examples.english: The towel is dry and the tablecloth is white.
The public library is organising a Greek evening.

sections.title: Similar masculine endings, different feminine forms
paragraphs: `Doux` becomes `douce` (soft/gentle), `roux` becomes `rousse` (red-haired), and `jaloux` becomes `jalouse` (jealous). `Faux` becomes `fausse` (false), not `fause`. Masculine forms ending in `x` already have that same spelling in the plural; feminine plurals add `s`.

Other useful pairs are `frais/fraîche` (fresh/cool), `long/longue` (long), `favori/favorite` (favourite) and `rigolo/rigolote` (funny, informal). The 1990 spelling `fraiche` without a circumflex is also accepted. `Rigolo` is conversational; `amusant` is a less informal alternative.
points: `Frais/fraîche/frais/fraîches`; `long/longue/longs/longues`; `favori/favorite/favoris/favorites`; `rigolo/rigolote/rigolos/rigolotes`. Each set lists masculine singular, feminine singular, masculine plural, feminine plural.

examples.french: Ma sœur est **rousse**, et elle n'est pas **jalouse**.
examples.english: My sister is red-haired, and she is not jealous.

examples.french: Cette information est **fausse** ; l'attente sera plus **longue**.
examples.english: This information is false; the wait will be longer.

examples.french: Ma boisson **favorite** est fraîche ; cette histoire est **rigolote**.
examples.english: My favourite drink is cool; this story is funny.

mistakes.why: The feminine of `faux` has double `s`, followed by plural `s`.

practice.explanation: Both traditional and 1990 spellings are accepted.
Blanc gives blanche, then plural s.
Vif follows the f to ve family.

production_task.prompt: Describe a room or place you like using four relevant adjectives, not a disconnected list.
production_task.model_answer: Ma pièce favorite est la cuisine. Elle a une table neuve et de longues étagères blanches. La lumière est douce le matin. J'aime y prendre mon petit-déjeuner.
production_task.translation: My favourite room is the kitchen. It has a new table and long white shelves. The light is soft in the morning. I like having breakfast there.
rubric: Agree each adjective with its own noun.
Check irregular stems before adding plural `s`.
Use descriptions that help someone imagine the place.
